item.title: China's top diplomat calls for new 'golden decade' of Lancang-Mekong cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 11:04:00
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, co-chairs the 11th Lancang-Mekong Cooperation (LMC) Foreign Ministers' Meeting with Thai Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow in Beijing, capital of China, Nov. 4, 2026. Cambodian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Prak Sokhonn, Lao Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Thongsavanh Phomvihane, Vietnamese Foreign Minister Le Hoai Trung and Myanmar's Minister for the Ministry of National Planning, Investment and Foreign Economic Relations, Aung Kyaw Hoe, attended the meeting here on Wednesday. (Xinhua/Tian Yu) Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi on Wednesday called on the six Lancang-Mekong countries to build on their fruitful cooperation in the past 10 years and jointly usher in a new "golden decade." Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, made the remarks when co-chairing with Thai Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow the 11th Lancang-Mekong Cooperation (LMC) Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Beijing. The LMC mechanism was launched by the six countries in 2016. Its name derives from a river known as the Lancang in China and the Mekong after it flows out of the country and through Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam. China stands ready to work with Mekong countries in the direction set by the leaders, take stronger measures and more coordinated steps, to continuously substantiate the Lancang-Mekong community with a shared future, Wang said. Wang called for efforts to keep Lancang-Mekong Cooperation at the forefront of regional cooperation, make it a benchmark for Global South solidarity, and contribute to building a community with a shared future for humanity. Lancang-Mekong countries should strengthen top-level design on core issues such as regional development and security, enhance the alignment of development strategies, promote trade and investment liberalization and facilitation, and deliver more "small and beautiful" livelihood demonstration projects to give people a greater sense of gain, he said. It is important to expand cooperation in emerging fields such as the digital economy, artificial intelligence, smart manufacturing and smart agriculture, he said, welcoming more Mekong countries to join the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO). He urged Lancang-Mekong countries to oppose external interference and incitement of bloc confrontation, reject the creation of exclusive "small circles," and never allow the resurgence of militarism, adding that the countries should step up joint efforts to combat cross-border crimes. Wang suggested the countries promote the establishment of a Lancang-Mekong cross-border disaster early-warning cooperation mechanism and jointly enhance disaster prevention, mitigation and relief capabilities. Cambodian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Prak Sokhonn, Lao Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Thongsavanh Phomvihane, Vietnamese Foreign Minister Le Hoai Trung and Myanmar's Minister for the Ministry of National Planning, Investment and Foreign Economic Relations, Aung Kyaw Hoe, attended the meeting. All parties at the meeting spoke highly of the positive progress of the LMC over the past decade and appreciated China's important leading role in advancing their cooperation. Those present reaffirmed their commitment to good-neighborliness and friendship, mutual respect and mutual trust, deeper cooperation and win-win outcomes, and to jointly promoting sustainable development and prosperity in the region. They agreed to deepen cooperation in priority areas such as connectivity, water resources and environment, expand digital transformation, green innovation, and promote people-to-people and cultural exchanges. They also agreed to strengthen disaster governance, tighten security coordination, combat cross-border crimes and safeguard regional tranquility. All parties agreed to maintain close communication to ensure that the fifth LMC Leaders' Meeting is a complete success and delivers positive outcomes. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, co-chairs the 11th Lancang-Mekong Cooperation (LMC) Foreign Ministers' Meeting with Thai Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow in Beijing, capital of China, Nov. 4, 2026. Cambodian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Prak Sokhonn, Lao Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Thongsavanh Phomvihane, Vietnamese Foreign Minister Le Hoai Trung and Myanmar's Minister for the Ministry of National Planning, Investment and Foreign Economic Relations, Aung Kyaw Hoe, attended the meeting here on Wednesday. (Xinhua/Tian Yu)

item.title: China's highest-altitude ultra-supercritical coal-fired power unit starts operations, set to bolster grid stability
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 09:40:00
An aerial view of China's highest-altitude ultra-supercritical coal-fired power project in Golmud, Northwest China's Qinghai Province, whose first unit began commercial operations on November 5, 2026. Photo: Screenshot from CCTV China's highest-altitude ultra-supercritical coal-fired electricity project began commercial operations on Thursday after its first generating unit completed a 168-hour trial run, marking a breakthrough in coal power generation under challenging high-altitude conditions, state broadcaster CCTV News reported. Located in Golmud, Northwest China's Qinghai Province, at an average altitude of about 2,850 meters, the power project comprises two 660-megawatt ultra-supercritical generating units. It is designed to provide reliable electricity supplies while helping balance fluctuations in renewable energy generation. Once both units are operational, the project is expected to generate 6 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity annually, enough to meet the yearly electricity needs of approximately 6.6 million residents, Zhao Falin, the project's chief manager at Huadian Golmud Co, said. He added that the project would strengthen the stability and reliability of Qinghai's power grid while providing flexible back-up capacity to support the large-scale integration of renewable energy. It’s not easy to build a coal-fired power plant at such an altitude. Low oxygen levels and atmospheric pressure make it harder for coal to burn efficiently, while the high alkali content of the fuel can cause slagging and ash buildup in boilers. To overcome these challenges, the project introduced oxygen-assisted startup and combustion-stabilization technologies for ultra-low-load operations. The customized boiler system enables the plant to burn high-alkali coal while flexibly adjusting its output to match changing electricity demand, addressing key technical hurdles in high-altitude coal power generation and filling a gap in the industry, according to the report. Ultra-supercritical technology allows coal-fired power plants to generate electricity using steam at exceptionally high temperatures and pressures, typically above 580 C and 24 megapascals. By extracting more energy from the same amount of coal, the technology improves efficiency, reduces fuel consumption and helps lower emissions. The Golmud plant's coal consumption per unit of electricity supplied is better than China's national benchmark, the CCTV News report said. The project incorporates water-saving and waste-management technologies. By treating and reusing reclaimed municipal wastewater from Golmud, the plant has established a closed-loop water management system that achieves zero wastewater discharge. It also reports a 100 percent comprehensive utilization rate for solid waste. Preparations are now underway for the second unit's full-system startup, with the project aiming to bring both units into commercial operation by the end of the year, according to the report. Global Times

item.title: Chinese consulate warns Chinese nationals of arbitrary questioning, detention risks at Honolulu airport
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 08:48:00
Passengers are seen at Daniel K. Inouye International Airport on January 2, 2026. Photo: VCG A number of Chinese nationals arriving in the US through Daniel K. Inouye International Airport have been subjected to arbitrary questioning and harassment by US border enforcement officers, had their visas revoked and been deported, the Chinese Consulate General in Los Angeles said in a travel advisory on Thursday. During the process, their electronic devices were searched, and they were detained for extended periods, denied contact with the outside world, and transferred to the Federal Detention Center in Honolulu while awaiting deportation flights. The Consulate General attaches great importance to protecting the safety and legitimate rights and interests of Chinese nationals, and has lodged solemn representations with the US side on multiple occasions over these incidents, according to the advisory. In view of the risks of arbitrary questioning, harassment and detention faced by Chinese nationals seeking lawful entry through the airport, the Consulate General advises Chinese nationals planning to travel to the US to exercise caution when choosing this airport as their port of entry. Chinese nationals are also advised to familiarize themselves in advance with US entry requirements and make thorough preparations. If questioned by US border enforcement officers, they should remain calm and respond rationally. If they do not understand the questions asked by the officers, they may request the assistance of an interpreter to avoid being misled, the Consulate General said. Global Times

item.title: When Singles' Day shoppers start stocking up on AI tokens, the time has changed: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 00:30:00
Concept picture of Token Photo: VCG As ordinary Chinese consumers embrace AI and enjoy the convenience of stockpiling tokens through e-commerce livestreams, and as humanoid robots and green manufacturing emerge as new showcases of China's intelligent manufacturing capabilities and Chinese modernization, an increasing number of Western media outlets and scholars are coming to recognize a remarkable reality: "The future is in China." This year's Double 11, or Singles' Day, shopping festival has brought a new item to Chinese consumers' shopping lists: Token. Tmall and JD.com have each introduced AI token sections bringing together services from Alibaba Cloud, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI and Zhipu AI. One livestream even recorded sales of 2 trillion tokens in just half an hour. The fact that AI tokens have become one of the headline products on e-commerce platforms is a phenomenon rarely seen anywhere else in the world. Foreign media have taken notice, expressing both curiosity and astonishment. There was a time when Americans were driving cars, watching television and eating fried chicken, while the "four big things" in Chinese households were watches, bicycles, sewing machines and radios. It was not until the late 1970s that televisions, refrigerators and washing machines began to find their way into a limited number of Chinese homes. In those days, the West had the power to set the standard for what constituted "modern living," and its way of life was widely regarded as the model for the future. China's priority was to catch up with industrialization, bringing within reach of ordinary households products that had long been commonplace elsewhere. Few could have imagined that, decades later, China would be at the forefront of the widespread adoption of smart devices, mobile payments and digital services. Fewer even could have predicted that China would become a force in defining new forms of consumption, new standards and even new ways of life in the latest wave of digital transformation. The same transformation is also unfolding in digital technology. A new digital product or concept would often first take shape in Silicon Valley before gradually spreading to the rest of the world. But the appearance of tokens on Singles' Day shopping shelves has challenged this long-established pattern. Tokens are no longer simply another overseas concept or business model replicated in China. Instead, the token-based consumption has emerged from the combined forces of China's vast digital consumer market, highly active user base and mature industrial ecosystem. Just a few years ago, some Western commentators were still quick to question China's capacity for digital innovation, arguing that it could make only incremental advances in applications but would never forge its own path in foundational technologies. Yet the rapid uptake of open-source large language models, the gradual deployment of humanoid robots in industrial settings, and now the arrival of digital resources in the mass consumer market tell a different story. The world is witnessing an innovation hub capable of continually defining new demands and creating new applications. As ordinary Chinese consumers embrace AI and enjoy the convenience of stockpiling tokens through e-commerce livestreams, and as humanoid robots and green manufacturing emerge as new showcases of China's intelligent manufacturing capabilities and Chinese modernization, an increasing number of Western media outlets and scholars are coming to recognize a remarkable reality: "The future is in China." Today, AI is not only directly driving consumption of smart devices and related hardware, but the "AI Plus" initiative is also deeply empowering the rapid development of sectors such as education, healthcare, elderly care, culture and tourism, employment, and consumer services. As AI enters millions of households and empowers thousands of industries, a more competitive AI consumer ecosystem will bring more affordable tokens and a wider range of application scenarios. Underpinning this transformation is China's rapid progress in AI foundation models, cloud computing, and the chip application ecosystem. China is developing distinctive competitive advantages in the global AI race. According to OpenRouter, a global AI model aggregation platform, Chinese large language models have outpaced their US counterparts in token usage for 27 consecutive weeks, including the week of October 26 to November 1. More than one-third of the tokens used by enterprises in the Global South countries come from Chinese models. Increasingly, the decisive factor in AI competition is whether companies can consistently deliver reliable, practical AI services to businesses and consumers at reasonable costs, and whether technological advances can be translated into productivity gains across industries. Why has China been among the first to develop an ecosystem for token consumption? The answer is simple: the public's high level of acceptance has accelerated the development of the ecosystem, while a mature ecosystem has, in turn, further reinforced positive public attitudes. A 2025 KPMG survey covering 47 countries found that Chinese people were among the most optimistic about AI. From electronic payments to e-commerce and food delivery, from short videos to intelligent driving, and now to access to highly cost-effective AI tokens, Chinese consumers have undoubtedly been at the forefront of enjoying the benefits of the intelligent era. This positive, self-reinforcing ecosystem is the natural outcome of China's remarkable rise in comprehensive national strength and the broad improvement in its population's educational and cultural attainment over the past several decades. From the "four big things" and "three big things" that once symbolized household prosperity to the integration of digital technologies into everyday consumption today, the Chinese people's pursuit of a better life has never changed. What has changed is our ability and approach to fulfill that aspiration. Today, we are turning the possibilities of a new era of digital civilization into experiences that benefit billions of people globally. This transformation has not been driven by exploitation, coercion, or the erection of barriers, but by practical efforts to ensure that ordinary people can genuinely and equally share in the benefits of technological progress.

item.title: 2026 Kuliang Forum opens in Fuzhou, spotlighting lasting bonds between Chinese and American people
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04 22:38:00
The 2026 Kuliang Forum kicks off in Fuzhou, East China's Fujian Province, on November 4, 2026. Source: Courtesy of People's Daily Digital Communication Co., Ltd. The 2026 Kuliang Forum, organized by People's Daily Digital Communication Co., Ltd., opened in Fuzhou, East China's Fujian Province, on Wednesday, bringing together guests from China and the US to explore ways to strengthen people-to-people ties and advance practical cooperation. For the first time, the forum was held in the city where the century-old Kuliang story began. Under the theme of "Moving Towards Each Other," participants at this year's forum shared their perspectives on the history and future of China-US friendship, how language and cultural exchanges can bring people closer, and the importance of providing young people with more opportunities to meet, learn from and work with one another. At the opening ceremony on Wednesday morning, Yu Shaoliang, president of People's Daily, said that as a flagship platform for people-to-people and cultural exchanges between China and the US, this year's forum would bring together forces for closer engagement and open new paths for cooperation, friendship and the future. He expressed hope that people from all sectors in both countries would be guided by the important consensus reached by the two heads of state, share more stories of friendship, voice greater support for cooperation, and deepen mutual understanding and mutual trust. He also called on media organizations, think tanks, universities, businesses and local communities in both countries to use the forum as a bridge for deeper exchanges and cooperation in education, science and technology, trade and culture, encouraging more frequent visits and interactions between the two peoples and helping them build closer ties. Through sincere dialogue and exchanges, he said, the two sides should work to deliver more practical results that benefit the people of both countries and contribute to global development, achieve mutual benefit and win-win outcomes, and further strengthen the momentum for China-US friendship. Zhao Long, secretary of the Fujian Provincial Committee of the Communist Party of China (CPC), and Qin Haixiang, secretary of the Fuzhou Municipal Committee of the CPC, also attended the forum and delivered remarks. US participants highlighted how language learning, shared experiences and everyday interactions help build personal connections. "People-to-people exchanges should not be like visiting an aquarium," said Eric Chipman, executive director of the Helen Foster Snow Foundation and Gung Ho Programs, speaking in Chinese at the forum. He argued that genuine connections could only be built when people went beyond observing one another and found opportunities to take part in each other's lives and work toward shared goals. In an interview with the Global Times, Chipman said a major challenge was Americans' limited exposure to China. Drawing on his nearly two decades of experience organizing China-US exchange programs, he said firsthand experiences could profoundly change young people's perspectives. "When they come here, they can't view the world the same way ever again," he said, adding that some former student participants had gone on to study or work in China or encourage others to visit. Chipman described Kuliang's history as a reminder of the long-standing connections between the two countries. He also expressed interest in bringing American students to Kuliang in the future, saying, "That would be incredible." Other US participants also shared their thoughts on how to foster understanding between the two peoples, drawing on their own experiences and areas of interest. Trenton Marsolek, a 27-year-old Tsinghua University alumnus, visited Kuliang for the first time during the trip. He told the Global Times that the Kuliang story and the friendship it represents carry significant meaning for China-US relations. He said friendships between Chinese and American people had endured through changing historical circumstances. To promote greater mutual understanding, Marsolek said more young Americans should visit China and experience the country firsthand. He said young people did not need to begin conversations with complicated political or philosophical topics. "At the end of the day, we're all human," he said, adding that conversations about ordinary topics help people see one another as individuals and build mutual understanding. For Vivian, a Chinese-American student at Peking University's School of Chinese as a Second Language, the forum was particularly meaningful given her work in teaching Chinese to international students. She told the Global Times that language learning cannot be separated from culture, real-life settings and stories. The forum offers American students and other visitors an opportunity not only to learn about Kuliang and its history, but also to experience Chinese culture firsthand. Drawing on her experience in Chinese language education, Vivian stressed that people need to interact with one another in order to develop genuine understanding. Such exchanges, she said, can help American students and business visitors gain a deeper appreciation of Chinese culture. This year's forum also featured roundtable discussions and youth exchange activities. Participants discussed the importance of constructive relations between major countries, the lessons of history for China-US relations and ways to deepen friendship between the two peoples. During the event, a new book, Bond with Kuliang: Stories of China-US Friendship and Cooperation , was launched, while an accompanying photo exhibition was held featuring images documenting exchanges and friendship between people in China and the US. Since its launch in 2024, the Kuliang Forum has held two editions in Beijing and New York, bringing together more than 300 participants from various sectors in China and the US. The forum has become a platform for dialogue and exchange between people from both countries.

item.title: GT Voice: Why resisting US pressure matters for South Korean chipmakers
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04 22:26:00
Production of semiconductor chip File photo: VCG Washington's efforts to attract South Korean chip investment risk being undermined by its own restrictions. Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that US officials have held up approval for American chipmaking equipment needed by SK hynix to expand its production in China, complicating the South Korean chipmaker's plans for new memory-chip plants in the state of New York. According to Reuters, SK hynix is seeking US export licenses to equip its plant in Dalian, Northeast China's Liaoning Province, arguing that increased production there would help fund its planned US expansion. Negotiations are ongoing, with the outcome uncertain. But the episode already exposes tension in US-South Korea chip "cooperation." Washington wants to attract more South Korean investment and manufacturing capacity to the US, while its export controls constrain South Korean chipmakers' ability to expand its production in China. This reveals a divergence of interests: Washington is seeking to strengthen its own semiconductor industry, even at the potential expense of South Korean companies' commercial interests. For a fuller picture of the pressure facing South Korean chipmakers, a September report by The Korea Herald is worth revisiting. It said that Washington had revived its push for targeted semiconductor tariffs, raising pressure on Samsung Electronics and SK hynix to expand US production or face duties on chips made overseas. If South Korean chipmakers expand their US operations under such pressure, a growing share of investment, advanced manufacturing capacity and high-value jobs could accrue to the US rather than South Korea. This raises a question about whether such "cooperation" truly serves both sides' interests. Washington stands to gain new investment and jobs, while South Korean companies face constraints on their global operations and risk seeing more of their industrial capabilities move overseas. The arrangement appears to put US industrial interests first, leaving South Korea to bear much of the commercial and strategic cost. On its US investment plans, South Korean media outlet AJP reported on Wednesday that SK hynix had yet to finalize any specific plans for new semiconductor manufacturing facilities in the US. SK hynix also said that it was continuing to bring US-made semiconductor manufacturing equipment into its Dalian plant under an existing export license, while negotiations over next year's authorization remain underway, AJP reported. Why are these Chinese factories so important to South Korean chipmakers? The Korea JoongAng Daily reported in August that SK hynix's plant in Wuxi, East China's Jiangsu Province, accounts for 40 percent of its total dynamic random-access memory output, while its Dalian plant accounts for 30 percent of its total NAND output. At a time of strong global demand and tight memory-chip supply, China's production capacity is a valuable asset for South Korean chipmakers. Retaining access to this capacity is plainly in the commercial interests of these companies. China's value also lies in its mature industrial ecosystem. Its extensive supplier networks and manufacturing capabilities have long supported South Korean chipmakers' global operations. This has been a mutually beneficial arrangement, with South Korean companies drawing on China's industrial base while contributing investment to the wider supply chain. Yet Washington is putting South Korean chipmakers in a difficult position. While seeking to attract their investment to the US, it is also trying to limit their ability to expand production in China. In doing so, Washington is putting its geopolitical objectives ahead of South Korean companies' commercial interests. South Korean chipmakers should not accommodate US demands at the expense of their global operations. They have every reason to preserve the flexibility to make investment and production decisions based on commercial considerations. China's semiconductor industry is advancing rapidly, creating new competitive pressures for South Korean chipmakers. But competition does not preclude cooperation where interests remain aligned. The question is whether South Korean chipmakers can withstand US pressure without sacrificing the global reach and commercial flexibility on which their competitiveness depends. That balance will have consequences well beyond their operations in China.

item.title: 9-year CIIE: An open China responds to surge of protectionism with tangible dividends
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04 20:41:00
A ceremony marking the arrival of the first batch of exhibits for the upcoming 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE) is held at the National Exhibition and Convention Center (Shanghai), the main venue for the CIIE, in east China's Shanghai on October 26, 2026. Photo: Xinhua On November 5, the 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE) will kick off in Shanghai. The fact that the event has been held as scheduled for nine consecutive years is, in itself, a powerful declaration of openness. This year's expo brings together 162 countries, regions, and international organizations, with 4,142 overseas companies participating. For the first time, the number of Fortune 500 companies and industry leaders among the exhibitors has exceeded 300, and nearly 200 companies and institutions have participated in all nine editions of the expo. One of the most intriguing highlights of this year's CIIE comes from the US delegation. For the eighth consecutive year, US companies have occupied the largest exhibition space among all participating countries, with their exhibition area increasing by another 1,500 square meters compared to the previous edition. Even as Washington's policy toolkit is filled with tariff barriers and "small yards, high fences" approach, US companies continue to showcase cutting-edge innovations on this platform, aiming to foster a mutually beneficial relationship with the Chinese market. "The power of the market is robust," said Zhou Mi, a senior researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation under the Ministry of Commerce. "US companies are not just chasing short-term gains by participating in the expo; they are also exploring opportunities for deeper cooperation. Amid global market volatility and supply chain pressures, China boasts both growth potential and supply chain resilience. That explains the core reason behind this contrast - "policymakers build walls, yet businesses show up." World premieres and first-time exhibitions are the most distinctive hallmarks of the CIIE. During the first eight sessions of the CIIE, more than 3,400 new products, technologies, and services made their global or regional debuts. This year, there are over 480 representative exhibits making their global, Asian, or China debuts - a record high - which reflects this mutual engagement in innovation. Zhou Mi told the Global Times that innovation is key for companies to generate profits and capture market share. The decision to launch a large number of new products in China stems from the potential of the Chinese market and its advantages in industrial support systems. Tu Xinquan, Dean of the China Institute for WTO Studies at the University of International Business and Economics, believes that as one of the world's largest consumer markets, China ranks among the global leaders in domestic consumer acceptance of new technologies and products. Making China the launchpad, testing ground, and promotion hub for their innovations is a highly strategic choice for innovative enterprises. The appeal of the CIIE also stems from tangible orders and growth dividends. The cumulative intended transaction value from the first eight editions exceeded $580 billion, with the eighth edition alone recording $83.49 billion in intended transactions - a 4.4 percent year-over-year increase. Take Takeda Pharmaceutical as an example. From a mid-sized company at its first exhibition, it has grown into one of the top 10 multinational pharmaceutical companies in China, with cumulative investment in the country exceeding 3 billion yuan. Turning exhibits into products and exhibitors into investors represents the tangible, concrete, and graspable opportunities in China for the global business community. Tu believes that China is committed to independent, high-level opening-up, and the CIIE serves as a key window through which China proactively embraces the world. "At a time when anti-globalization sentiments are on the rise and global trade and the economy are fraught with uncertainty, China has continued to host the expo year after year, injecting stability into turbulent global trade and serving as a stabilizer for the world economy," Tu said. He added that the CIIE also builds a bridge connecting high-quality international supply with domestic consumption upgrades, driving the optimization of domestic supply and unleashing the potential of domestic consumption. "It is hoped that China's practice of opening up will inspire more countries to safeguard the multilateral free trade system." The CIIE's cooperative philosophy is based on equality and mutual benefit, without distinction by nationality or alignment with any bloc: Developed countries showcase cutting-edge technologies, emerging markets demonstrate their vibrant dynamism, and least-developed economies receive support here. This year's event continues to support least developed countries, with the amount of free exhibition space allocated to them increasing by 17 percent year-on-year; distinctive agricultural products from African nations such as Tanzania and Benin have found stable sales channels here. Rwanda is a prime example. The country went from bringing samples in a suitcase to now shipping a steady stream of local agricultural products to China by container. Developed economies, emerging markets, and least developed countries are all participating on an equal footing, standing in stark contrast to exclusive, "closed-circle" economic and trade arrangements. Zhou said the CIIE provides a platform for countries to exchange ideas and learn from one another, where different stakeholders can engage in dialogue and inspire each other. This diverse and inclusive framework is a concrete demonstration of China's commitment to treating all trading partners equally, upholding the principle of most-favored-nation treatment. Over the past five years, China's contribution to global economic growth has remained stable at around 30 percent, exceeding the combined contribution of the G7 nations. Today's "China Opportunities 2.0" places greater emphasis on innovation and collaboration, institutional openness, and full-chain co-construction. The continuously expanding scale of the US delegation at the expo confirms a simple truth: Businesses vote with their feet, and market forces are difficult to completely block with geopolitical barriers. The value of the CIIE's 9-year commitment lies in its steadfastness. While tariffs can artificially inflate transaction costs, they cannot stem the drive of global capital, innovation, and goods to find markets. The message the CIIE continues to send is clear and resolute: The doors to the Chinese market will remain open to all partners willing to cooperate on an equal footing.

item.title: Scholars from around the world trace Silk Road history in Xinjiang
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04 12:43:00
A scholar from Pakistan shares research findings at the symposium titled Towards Anxi from Afar: Academic Symposium on Qiuci Studies, in Urumqi, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, Oct. 31, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Yuanhao) Once a thriving crossroads on the Silk Road in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, the ancient kingdom of Kucha has left traces of its rich history in museums and collections around the world. Buddhist murals, sculptures and manuscripts from the Kucha kingdom, also known as the ancient Qiuci State ("Qiuci" being its Chinese pinyin form), are now held in Berlin, St. Petersburg, Tokyo and elsewhere. Reconstructing its past is therefore requiring researchers to work across borders and pool their expertise. Understanding Kucha's past has become an international scholarly effort. The shared pursuit brought more than 180 scholars from 15 countries and regions to Urumqi, capital of Xinjiang, for a two-day symposium, titled Towards Anxi from Afar: Academic Symposium on Qiuci Studies, which concluded on Sunday. Scholars from China, Britain, Germany, Italy, Japan, Pakistan and elsewhere exchanged research findings on ancient texts, religion, archaeology and cultural heritage conservation. Located between the Tianshan Mountains and the Taklimakan Desert, the ancient Kucha region encompassed parts of today's Kuqa, Baicheng, Xayar and Xinhe in Xinjiang. For centuries, it was a meeting point of civilizations. Chinese silk and paper traveled westward along trade routes, while Buddhism from India, Persian artistic influences and Sogdian merchants made their way east. At the symposium, Rong Xinjiang, a professor at Peking University and president of the Chinese Dunhuang-Turpan Society, presented new research on a tomb epitaph unearthed in Kuqa in 2025. For overseas researchers, keeping up with archaeological discoveries in Xinjiang is an important reason to maintain close ties with Chinese scholars. "Continued contact with colleagues around the world, especially in China, is essential," said Caren Dreyer, a researcher at the Museum of Asian Art in Berlin. "It enables us to keep abreast of new findings and to participate actively in the international scholarly community." For Erica Hunter, a scholar from the University of Cambridge who specializes in relics and Syriac manuscripts excavated from Turpan, the value of such gatherings lies in bringing together evidence that would otherwise remain separated by geography. Russian scholars can share materials from St. Petersburg, while German researchers can discuss those in Berlin, Hunter said. Equally important are the different interpretations scholars bring to their research. Hunter has visited Xinjiang several times over the past four years to share her research on Syriac manuscripts discovered in the region. She said such exchanges help scholars overcome barriers and learn from one another. "It's a two-way process, and that's very important." On his first visit to Xinjiang, Pakistani scholar Fawad Khan followed the presentations with keen interest. He said the symposium offered a valuable learning opportunity for scholars. The exchanges also reflected a growing emphasis on international collaboration in Silk Road studies, as Chinese institutions expand academic cooperation in fields ranging from Turpan and Qiuci studies, to research on the ancient city of Beiting. For Italian scholar Erica Forte, the symposium was also a reunion. Speaking Chinese with colleagues, she caught up with old friends and professors who had supported her during her studies. For her, the conversations reflected what had long given the Silk Road its significance, namely connections between people and cultures, as scholars came together to exchange findings, compare perspectives and deepen their understanding of a kingdom that once stood at the crossroads of civilizations. Erica Hunter, a scholar from the University of Cambridge, attends the symposium titled Towards Anxi from Afar: Academic Symposium on Qiuci Studies, in Urumqi, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, Oct. 31, 2026.
